source.quote: The experiment was conducted aboard the International Space Station (ISS) inside the Microgravity Glove Box (MSG).
After every 2 burns the MSG Work Volume must be purged for 3 minutes

one_line: Astronauts burned small fabric strips, plastic spheres and slabs, and wax candles in a gentle, adjustable air stream on the ISS to see whether solids burn more readily without gravity than in the Earth-based test NASA uses to approve materials, and whether a puff of nitrogen puts the flames out.
summary: BASS (Burning and Suppression of Solids) burned 41 small solid samples in about 115 burns inside a 76 mm square flow duct in the ISS Microgravity Science Glovebox in 2012-2013, at about 1 atm and 16-23% O2. Fuels were a cotton-fibreglass (SIBAL) fabric, Nomex and Ultem sheets, PMMA spheres and slabs, and wax candles, in fan-driven air flows from below 1 to about 44 cm/s, with an upstream nitrogen jet of up to 500 cc/min. The fabric, which cannot burn downward in 1 g air, spread steadily in 9-10 cm/s opposed flow. Opposed spread peaked at 10-15 cm/s; concurrent spread rose linearly with flow (2.55 versus 1.21 mm/s opposed at about 10 cm/s), and concurrent flames quenched below 1 cm/s. PMMA and candle flames survived for minutes as dim blue flames near 1 cm/s. The nitrogen jet usually removed only the leading edge, and most flames went out only when the airflow stopped. Fire-retarded Nomex HT90-40 and Ultem did not burn at 21-22% O2. Normal-gravity screening therefore does not bound flammability in every configuration.

question.text: BASS tested the hypothesis that a solid with adequate ventilation burns as well as, or better than, the same material in normal gravity at the same pressure, O2 concentration and temperature. If true, NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 (an upward-burning 1-g test used to screen spacecraft materials) would offer less safety margin than assumed. Testing anything but the thinnest fuels needs minutes of microgravity, which drop towers and parabolic aircraft cannot give. The investigation had two objectives. (1) Begin to bridge the gap between the 1-g Test 1 method, ground-based microgravity tests and actual flammability in space, using practical, thicker fuels and wake flames (flames sheltered behind an object). (2) Assess how well an inert gaseous agent (nitrogen, similar to the ISS extinguisher agent) puts out flames over different materials, geometries, preheat states and flows. Behind the second objective is the worry that in microgravity the best place to aim a suppressant is unclear, and a jet might even feed the flame by entraining air.

sources.quote: If this hypothesis is true, it implies serious safety concerns over the utility and margin of safety provided NASA- STD-6001 Test #1.
it is possible that the suppressant stream will be ineffective or might actually make the flame worse through the entrainment of oxygen.
As a result, the 1-g test currently used by NASA to rate materials for space may need to be re-evaluated from a margin-of-safety point of view.

physics.text: A flame spreading over a solid heats the unburnt fuel ahead of it until the fuel pyrolyses. The vapour then mixes with oxygen and burns. On Earth, buoyancy drives an induced flow past the flame of order tens of cm/s (the BASS authors give about 20 cm/s at the flame zone for their fabric). In orbit, buoyancy is essentially absent, so the only flow is what the ventilation imposes, and that can be just a few cm/s. Two flow directions matter. In opposed flow the air moves against the direction of spread (downward burning on Earth), and spread is controlled by heat conducted forward from a small region at the flame's leading edge. In concurrent flow the air moves with the spread (upward burning on Earth), and the whole flame and hot plume preheat the fuel, so the flame can grow. A thin fuel's flammability boundary, plotted against flow speed, is U-shaped. At high flow, finite-rate chemistry fails and the flame blows off. At very low flow, the flame's heat release falls until radiative loss is a significant fraction of it, and the flame quenches. The low-flow quenching branch lies below the 1-g buoyant flow limit, so it can only be observed in microgravity. Between the branches there can be conditions, such as moderate opposed flows, where a material that self-extinguishes on Earth burns steadily in orbit. Inert-gas suppression works by diluting the oxygen and adding heat capacity at the flame. In microgravity, however, a jet also adds momentum and can entrain surrounding air, so where and how the agent is delivered matters.

sources.quote: This quenching extinction occurs when the flame power output decreases, and the radiative heat loss rate becomes a significant fraction of the total combustion heat release from the flame.
The observation of the quenching extinction branch is only possible at microgravity, since otherwise any buoyant flow generated would take the system out of the low-speed flow regime.
Normal gravity studies are limited to flow speeds above the minimum buoyant speed in the flame zone (20 cm/s for this system).
For concurrent-flow flames, the fuel preheating depends on the entire flame and hot plume which means that the flame response time to flow changes is a strong function of the flame size.
For a fire burning in microgravity, the best point of application of suppressant may not be immediately apparent, especially for a partially obstructed flame or a wake-stabilized flame.

equations.meaning: Thermal-regime (de Ris) spread rate of an opposed-flow flame over a thermally thin solid. $V_f$ spread rate (m/s); $\lambda_g$ gas thermal conductivity (W/m K); $T_f$ flame temperature, $T_v$ fuel vaporisation (pyrolysis) temperature, $T_\infty$ ambient temperature (K); $\rho_s$ solid density (kg/m3); $c_s$ solid specific heat (J/kg K); $\tau$ fuel half-thickness (m). Valid when gas-phase chemistry is fast compared with the flow residence time (large Damkohler number) and radiative losses are negligible; $V_f$ is then independent of the opposed flow speed. BASS opposed spread over SIBAL fabric instead peaked at 10-15 cm/s and fell on either side, so the BASS flows lie partly outside this regime: kinetic effects at higher flows, radiative losses at low flows.

Opposed-flow flame spread rate increases with flow to a maximum when the flow speed is around 10 to 15 cm/s and then decreases at higher speeds, in good agreement with previous research [Olson, 1991].

equations.meaning: Damkohler number at the flame leading edge: gas residence time over chemical time. $\alpha_g$ gas thermal diffusivity (m2/s); $U_r$ flow speed relative to the flame (m/s), with $U$ the imposed opposed flow and $V_f$ the spread rate; $\rho_g$ gas density (kg/m3); $Y_{O_2}$ oxygen mass fraction; $A$ pre-exponential factor of a one-step overall reaction (units such that the bracket is a rate in 1/s); $E$ activation energy (J/mol); $R$ gas constant (8.314 J/mol K); $T_f$ flame temperature (K). High-flow branch of the flammability boundary: the flame blows off when Da falls below a critical value, i.e. when $U_r$ is too large or O2 too low. On Earth the buoyant flow at the flame (about 20 cm/s for SIBAL) sets $U_r$, and downward spread over SIBAL blows off; in BASS, 9-10 cm/s opposed flow kept Da above critical, and no blow-off was reached up to about 44 cm/s. Order-of-magnitude scaling, not a fitted relation.

sources.quote: Normal gravity studies are limited to flow speeds above the minimum buoyant speed in the flame zone (20 cm/s for this system).
The explanation is that in normal gravity, the buoyant flow generated by the flame is too high for the flame to be supported and blowoff occurs.

equations.meaning: Radiative-loss fraction that controls the low-flow (quenching) branch. $\varepsilon$ effective emissivity of flame and hot surface; $\sigma$ Stefan-Boltzmann constant (5.67e-8 W/m2 K4); $A_f$ radiating area (m2); $\dot m_f$ fuel pyrolysis rate (kg/s); $\Delta h_c$ heat of combustion (J/kg); temperatures in K. As the forced flow falls towards zero in microgravity, oxygen supply and heat feedback weaken, the pyrolysis rate drops faster than the radiative loss, $\Phi_{rad}$ rises towards order one and the flame quenches. Buoyancy keeps $\Phi_{rad}$ small in 1 g, so this branch is observable only in microgravity. In BASS, concurrent SIBAL flames quenched below 1 cm/s, whereas PMMA and wax flames, fed by heat stored in the thick solid, stayed lit near 1 cm/s for minutes. Qualitative scaling, not fitted to BASS data.

sources.quote: This quenching extinction occurs when the flame power output decreases, and the radiative heat loss rate becomes a significant fraction of the total combustion heat release from the flame.
The observation of the quenching extinction branch is only possible at microgravity, since otherwise any buoyant flow generated would take the system out of the low-speed flow regime.

equations.meaning: Linear fits reported by the investigators to the steady base spread rate of concurrent-flow flames over SIBAL fabric (ISS cabin air, about 21-22% O2, about 1 atm), one fit per sample width (1 cm and 2 cm). $V_F$ flame-base spread rate (mm/s); $U_\infty$ imposed air speed (cm/s), plotted as negative for concurrent flow, so spread increases linearly with flow magnitude. At $U_\infty = -10$ cm/s the fits give 2.56 and 1.57 mm/s. The source does not label the fits by width; the first matches the 2.55 mm/s measured on a 2-cm sample at about 10 cm/s, and the second the 1.68 mm/s base speed of a 1-cm sample at 11 cm/s, so they are most likely the 2-cm and 1-cm fits respectively. Valid only within the flows tested; not near the quenching limit below about 1 cm/s.

sources.quote: Concurrent-flow flame spread rate increases linearly with flow speed, and linear curve fits are shown. Spread rate is width-dependent for the two widths studied.
Concurrent and Opposed Spread at ~ 10 cm/s 2.55 mm/s versus 1.21 mm/s

equations.meaning: Investigators' linear fits to flame-base and flame-tip position for a 1-cm-wide SIBAL sample in 11 cm/s concurrent flow on ISS (air, about 1 atm), after the initial growth phase (about 20 s). $x$ position along the sample (mm); $t$ time (s); $L_f$ flame length (mm). Base and tip advance at nearly the same speed (about 1.7 mm/s), so the flame has reached a steady (limiting) length, as predicted for purely forced concurrent flow at low speed. Valid only for this run.

Mean surface regression rate of a burning sphere from its mass-loss rate. $\dot r$ regression rate (m/s); $\dot m$ mean burning rate (kg/s); $\rho_s$ solid density (PMMA 1190 kg/m3); $r$ sphere radius (m). For the BASS 1-cm PMMA sphere (617.5 mg, consumed over four burns totalling 325 s at various flows), a NASA analysis gives $\dot m \approx$ 1.9 mg/s and $\dot r \approx$ 0.005 mm/s (0.3 mm/min). This is a lumped average over changing flow and a shrinking, reshaped sphere, not a local or steady value.

sources.quote: The total burn time was 5 min and 25 s (325 s). The average burning rate was 617.5/325 = 1.9 mg/s.

apparatus.text: The tests used the SPICE flow duct (76 mm x 76 mm cross-section), installed in the MSG, which supplied power, imaging and containment. A variable-speed fan with a flow straightener drove air through the duct at nominally 0-40 cm/s (the highest reading logged was about 44 cm/s). A hot-wire anemometer measured air speed, with a minimum measurable speed of 1 cm/s. The BASS control box let the crew turn the fan fully off, both as a safety measure and as a way to extinguish flames. Nitrogen from the MSG gaseous-nitrogen supply passed through a mass-flow controller (0-500 sccm) to a 3.2 mm nozzle upstream of the sample. Samples mounted on magnets in a sample-frame insert. Flat samples had an integral 29-gauge Kanthal wire igniter (about 1 ohm, about 3.7 A, ignition within about 2 s). Spheres, slabs and candles used bendable igniter wires that the crew positioned within about 1 mm of the fuel. Imaging was a Nikon D300s digital still camera looking through the top window at about 1 frame/s, and a colour video camera giving an edge view through the front window at 30 frames/s. A text overlay showed fan setting, air speed, radiometer output, nitrogen flow and time. A wide-angle radiometer measured flame radiation. Overlay parameters were logged at 4 Hz. In 2013 the MSG volume was vitiated with nitrogen, and the crew measured O2 with a CSA-CP (Compound Specific Analyzer - Combustion Products).

procedure.text: For each run the crew installed a sample, closed the duct and the MSG, and set the fan (and nitrogen flow, if used). They started video and still recording, then energised the igniter. For flat samples, flipping the holder 180 degrees put the igniter at the upstream end (opposed flow) or the downstream end (concurrent flow). After ignition the flame was left to burn, nominally for about 60 s in the original plan. For flat samples it usually burned until the fuel was consumed. Many runs changed the flow in steps during the burn. Opposed-flow flames re-reached steady spread within seconds, so one burn could give several flow conditions; concurrent flames respond too slowly for that. In suppression runs, nitrogen was raised in steps up to the maximum (about 495-500 cc/min). Flames that survived were put out by turning the air flow off. Afterwards the duct was cooled and vented: 2 min for thin samples and candles, 9 min for spheres and thick samples. The MSG was purged for 3 min after every 2 burns to dilute hydrogen fluoride (HF), a combustion by-product. Spheres, slabs and candles were re-ignited over several runs, so their shape changed from run to run. The 2012 runs were in ISS cabin air. Before many 2013 runs the MSG volume was diluted with nitrogen to about 16-18% O2, with O2 checked by CSA-CP. The ground team directed the runs in real time over audio and video links, and the crew's verbal observations were logged in the as-run test matrix.

psi_data.summary: PSI-26 holds 212 files (163.6 GB). Almost all of it (195 files, 162.5 GB) is raw imagery that has not been downloaded: 22 zips of 2012 still images (85.1 GB), and for 2013, 114 crew/downlink MP4 videos (22.8 GB) plus 37 zips (55.6 GB) of original images, XMP sidecars and text files. Raw data are organised by date. The data layout document describes 21 image galleries for 2012, and 12 audio/video collections plus 15 image galleries for 2013. No reduced data (spread rates, extinction points, digitised positions) are in PSI. Quantitative results exist only as plots and captions in the presentations and the 2013 US National Combustion Meeting paper. The most useful structured source is the as-run test matrix (xlsx). For each run it logs date and time, sample, igniter, fan and air settings, radiometer, GN2 setting, camera settings, cabin O2, pressure and CO2, and free-text crew/PI observations (outcome, extinction mode, soot). It links each run to its date folder in the raw data. The PSI experimental table CSV is a 6-column extract of it. No raw-data date folder exists before 2012-05-02, so the first 8 as-run tests (2012-03-30 to 2012-04-09) appear to have no imagery in PSI. Both final reports (BASS and SPICE) are listed but were not downloaded.

findings.claim: In opposed flow in microgravity (2-cm-wide SIBAL cotton-fibreglass fabric, ISS air, about 21-22% O2, about 1 atm), the flame reached steady spread within seconds of each flow change. Spread rate rose with flow to a maximum at about 10-15 cm/s and fell at higher speeds.

sources.quote: Opposed-flow flame spread rate increases with flow to a maximum when the flow speed is around 10 to 15 cm/s and then decreases at higher speeds, in good agreement with previous research [Olson, 1991].

sources.row: Excel rows 58-59 and 70-71, as-run 54, 55, 65, 66 (SIBAL), columns 'O2 % by volume' and 'pressure, atm'

findings.claim: The same SIBAL fabric cannot sustain downward (opposed-flow) spread in 1 g air: it ignites, then extinguishes, because the buoyant flow exceeds the blow-off limit. In microgravity at about 9-10 cm/s opposed flow it burned steadily over the whole sample. For this fabric and geometry, it is more flammable in microgravity than in 1 g, which supports the BASS hypothesis.

sources.quote: The fuel used in this investigation cannot burn in the downward (opposed-flow) configuration in normal gravity.
The explanation is that in normal gravity, the buoyant flow generated by the flame is too high for the flame to be supported and blowoff occurs.
Note: Downward flame spread (opposed flow) in 1-g with this material is not possible in normal air.

findings.claim: In concurrent flow, the base spread rate of SIBAL flames was constant within each run and increased linearly with flow speed, with different slopes for 1-cm and 2-cm widths. The plotted linear fits are V_F = -0.20 U + 0.56 and V_F = -0.15 U + 0.07 (V_F in mm/s, U in cm/s, concurrent flow plotted as negative U). The extracted text does not say which fit belongs to which width, but at 10-11 cm/s the first fit reproduces the 2.55 mm/s measured on a 2-cm sample and the second the 1.68 mm/s base speed of a 1-cm sample, so the steeper fit is most likely the 2-cm width.

sources.quote: Concurrent-flow flame spread rate increases linearly with flow speed, and linear curve fits are shown. Spread rate is width-dependent for the two widths studied.
Concurrent and Opposed Spread at ~ 10 cm/s 2.55 mm/s versus 1.21 mm/s

findings.claim: Concurrent-flow SIBAL flames reached a steady (limiting) length only below about 10 cm/s for the 2-cm-wide samples within the 8.5 cm sample length. At 10 cm/s and above, the flame tip was still accelerating. 1-cm-wide samples reached steady state, e.g. at 11 cm/s: after about 20 s, base and tip advanced in parallel at about 1.7 mm/s (fits x_base = 1.68 t - 13.81, x_tip = 1.71 t + 2.25, mm and s), with a flame length of about 16 mm.

sources.quote: However, only air flows less than 10 cm/s yield steady flame lengths.

findings.claim: Quenching (low-flow) extinction of a concurrent-flow SIBAL flame was observed when the flow was reduced in steps from 5 to about 1 cm/s. Extinction occurred at a low but finite flow below 1 cm/s. The authors present this as direct confirmation of the low-flow branch of the U-shaped flammability boundary for a thin fuel.

sources.quote: For concurrent flow, extinction was observed at a low but finite flow speed of less than 1 cm/s (shown by the dashed vertical line).

findings.claim: No opposed-flow quenching limit was reached: a 2-cm SIBAL flame stepped down from 10 to about 1 cm/s kept burning until the fuel ran out. findings.claim: The investigators' 2013 summary across all BASS sample types (17% to 21.5% O2, about 1 atm) is that flames were especially sensitive to air speed between 0 and 5 cm/s, and that the gas phase responded to flow changes almost without delay. Below 1 cm/s all flames became dim blue and very stable and, with little convective heat loss, could burn for a long time. Between about 1 and 5 cm/s the flame kept heating the solid, so fuel vaporisation rose and the flame grew stronger and more luminous with time. Only the smallest flames over acrylic slabs were visibly weakened by conductive loss to the solid, and even these burned for over 5 minutes before self-extinguishing.

sources.quote: Ambient oxygen atmospheres 17% to 21.5% (cabin air).
Microgravity flames were found to be especially sensitive to air flow speed in the range 0 to 5 cm/s.

At the lowest speeds examined (less than 1 cm/s) all the flames tended to become dim blue and very stable. However, heat loss at these very low convective rates is small so the flames can burn for a long time.

At moderate flow speeds (between about 1 and 5 cm/s) the flame continually heats the solid fuel resulting in an increasing fuel temperature, higher rate of fuel vaporization, and a stronger, more luminous flame as time progresses.
Only the smallest flames burning acrylic slabs appeared to be adversely influenced by solid conductive heat loss, but even these burned for over 5 minutes before self-extinguishing.

A 1-cm PMMA sphere (initial mass 617.5 mg) was fully consumed in four burns at various flow speeds totalling 325 s. That is an average burning rate of 1.9 mg/s, which the report converts to a mean regression rate of about 0.005 mm/s (0.3 mm/min), equivalent to a stretch rate of about 10 1/s.

relevance.text: Prevention and material selection: BASS shows directly that a material which self-extinguishes in the 1 g downward configuration can burn steadily in microgravity at realistic cabin ventilation speeds (about 10 cm/s). Flames over thin and thick fuels can also persist for minutes at flows of 1 cm/s or less. Normal-gravity screening therefore does not bound flammability in all configurations. On the other hand, the fire-retarded Ultem and Nomex HT90-40 behaved as in 1 g at 21-22% O2, and Nomex III burned only near its 1 g limiting O2. So the 1 g upward test was not shown to be non-conservative for the fire-retarded materials actually tested. These are qualitative, few-sample results at about 1 atm, not material flammability limits. Suppression: a nitrogen jet of up to about 500 cc/min from a fixed upstream nozzle generally removed only the leading edge of PMMA flames. Wake- and side-stabilised flames survived, apparently helped by air entrained by the jet, while shutting off the ventilation reliably extinguished small flames. This supports stopping ventilation as an effective response to small flames, and suggests the agent must reach the whole flame zone, including wake regions, not only the leading edge. The nozzle geometry and flow are specific to this hardware, so the agent quantities do not transfer to ISS extinguishers.

sources.quote: Normal gravity results cannot always be used to predict flame behavior and material flammability in spacecraft.
The standard test used by NASA to rate materials relies on burning them in an upward, normal-gravity configuration [NASA, 1998].

habitat_conditions.text: All runs were at ISS cabin pressure: 0.97-1.01 atm (98.3-102.2 kPa). In 2012, O2 was the uncontrolled cabin value, 20.9-22.7% by volume. In 2013 the MSG volume was diluted with nitrogen to 15.9-17.8% O2 for most runs; the rest were at about 20.5-21.2%. The logged O2 is sometimes the reading before vitiation, so a few 2013 runs logged near 21% actually burned at about 17%. BASS therefore covers normoxic and hypoxic (sub-21% O2) atmospheres at about the Earth sea-level reference (20.9% O2 at 101.3 kPa) only. It did not test the elevated-O2, reduced-pressure atmospheres of exploration: the shared reference for a Moon habitat is 30% O2 or more at 70.3 kPa (10.2 psi) or less, and a spacesuit is 100% O2 at 29.6 kPa (4.3 psi). Its highest O2 (22.7%) is below the Moon-habitat value, and its lowest pressure (98.3 kPa) is well above it. The SRD cites NASA CxP-70024 for such atmospheres but gives no values. BASS results cannot be applied to them without further tests or models. The flow range (below 1 to about 44 cm/s, mostly 0-20 cm/s) does span typical spacecraft ventilation speeds and the near-quiescent pockets behind equipment.

earth_benefits.text: Microgravity's simple, buoyancy-free flow field gives clean validation data for detailed flame-spread and extinction models. Once validated, these models can be extended to buoyant flames and used in designing fire detection and suppression systems on Earth. The team also cites the goal of a new or improved Earth-based flammability test method.

sources.quote: From a more fundamental point of view, improved combustion computational models using the experimental results can be developed to aid in the design of fire detection and suppression systems both in microgravity and on Earth.
It is highly desirable to develop a new and/or improved Earth-based test method for material flammability.

gaps: Final reports (PSI-26_Reports_BASS_FinalReport.pdf and PSI-26_Reports_SPICE_FinalReport.pdf) are listed in files.csv but not downloaded, and have no evidence chunks; the BASS final report is reported as unavailable from PSI (HTTP 404; not re-tested here). Both have the identical size of 553,693 bytes, so the 'BASS' report may be a duplicate of the SPICE report. To fill the gap, NTRS was searched: the ASGSR 2013 BASS talk (ntrs.nasa.gov 20140011099) and the BASS-II summary report NASA/TM-20210011385 (Appendix D gives BASS slab and sphere numbers; section 3.1 the leftover BASS candle) were used. The 9th USNCM 2015 fabric paper (ntrs.nasa.gov 20150008962) was read but reports mainly BASS-II runs, so it was not used for BASS findings.

No reduced numerical data (spread-rate tables, extinction flow speeds, sphere regression rates) are in PSI. Quantitative findings are limited to the fabric paper and its plot labels, plus one slab spread rate and one lumped sphere burning rate from NASA/TM-20210011385. For candles, nitrogen suppression and the 2013 low-O2 runs there are only image captions and as-run log notes. Searches of NTRS, Crossref and the web found no published BASS sphere, candle or nitrogen-suppression results: Takahashi et al., 'Burning Characteristics of Paraffin and Japan Wax Candle Flames in a Low-Speed Oxidizing Stream in Microgravity' (ASGSR 2013), Endo et al. PMMA-sphere papers (ASGSR 2014, 2016) and M. Endo's 2016 CWRU dissertation are cited in the TM but no accessible copy was found. The DOIs in the PSI record are mostly BASS-II or ground opposed-flow papers and add nothing on these topics.

The evidence parquet holds only the first rows of each As Run_Test Matrix.xlsx sheet. The full sheets were read directly from the xlsx, and facts from other rows are cited as psi_table sources with the Excel row number, as-run number and exact cell text (or an exact excerpt of it).

The extracted text does not assign the two concurrent-flow linear fits (V_F = -0.20U + 0.56, -0.15U + 0.07) to the 1-cm and 2-cm widths. The assignment given (steeper fit = 2 cm) is inferred from single-run values and should be confirmed from the figure.
Exploration-atmosphere values (O2 and pressure) are not given in any PSI-26 document; the SRD only cites NASA CxP-70024. The habitat comparison uses the shared values in docs/digest/reference.md.
Data quality: the PSI-26_Science Documents_Planned_Test Matrix.xlsx header row contains what appear to be account names and passwords (not reproduced here). It should be flagged to the PSI curators.
Data quality: the metadata zip is named 'PSI-26_metadata_PSI-102_BASS.zip', but PSI-102 is SAME (Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment). Its content is the PSI-26 record.

Data quality: the PSI record misspells Co-I Fumiaki Takahashi as 'Funiaki' and gives his affiliation as CWRU, while the presentations say NCSER. The 'approach' field is garbled ('measuring were used') and mentions 'cylinders', which appear in no other document (the candles-in-tubes are presumably meant).

Data quality (experimental table CSV): date typos ('6/29/`12', '5/15/2103'); GMT day 113 given for 4/26/2013 (should be 116) and 137 for 6/1/2013 (should be 152; the as-run sheet's own 'GMT 150' for the following rows is also inconsistent with 6/1); as-run numbers 24, 85 and 89-91 reused for different runs; one non-test 'SOOT Cleaning' row; sample labels in 2013 ('PMMA 2 cm') omit 'sphere'.

Data quality: Nomex naming is inconsistent. The SRD lists 'Nomex III (Blend)' and 'WSTF Nomex Natural (HT90-40)'. The as-run log uses 'Nomex blend 2 cm' and 'Nomex III Natural' / 'nomex natural III', and the 2013 overview says HT90-40 did not burn but Nomex III did. Which physical fabric burned (as-run 38, sample 29) is ambiguous.
Data quality: the 2012 ASGSR talk captions the 1-cm concurrent case as 10 cm/s and the 2013 talk and paper as 11 cm/s, with identical fit equations.

Raw-data coverage: no raw-data folder predates 2012-05-02, so imagery for as-run tests 1-8 (2012-03-30 to 2012-04-09) appears to be absent from PSI-26. The as-run 'Data without TP' sheet lists 2014 data folders (likely BASS-II, PSI-25) that are not among PSI-26 files. A 2013-07-09 raw folder falls after the last logged test (2013-06-01).

The PSI-26 file set includes engineering documents for SLICE (PSI-106), e.g. PSI-26_Engineering Documents_SLICE_SysReqDesignReview.pdf, and SPICE drawings. These were not used except to confirm the shared hardware.
